      When a word is contracted, or shortened, an apostrophe takes the place of the missing letter(s). Haven't is contracted from have not,so the apostrophe represents the o. 'Til is short for until so the u & n are represented by our little friend, the apostrophe.

    ↳ **@mohammadahmadian1314** (👍1 · 2019-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMFGv6wd5Y8&lc=UgyrtZXRfgMCYZR7qAR4AaABAg.8ulw31F1Xlo8vW7zd7d9fH
      Case1 : Bill's and Hillary's houses are beautiful.
      It means that Bill and Hillary live in two separate houses.
      Case2: Bill and Hillary's house is beautiful.
      It means that Bill and Hillary share a house with each other.
      Case3: Bill and Hillary's houses are beautiful.
      It means that Bill and Hillary possess two or more houses.
      As you can see there is no need to add apostrophe to house/houses. because houses do not possess anything. The owners are Bill and Hillary. Apostrophe goes to the word of owner.

  Here's my short story:
  
  This month has been a boring one. So, this morning I decided to go out and maybe ask over some of my friends to the bar. While I was trying to call one of my friends, Toni, someone knocked open the door. When I opened it, Toni was already there in front of my house.
  
  I asked, "what are you doing here, Toni? We're supposed to meet up at eight o'clock."
  
  Toni replied, "Hey, relax. I'm just going to pop in for few minutes. I need to tell you something." 
  
  Suddenly, I got confused and also mad because I still hadn't ask over my friends yet. Then, I asked "what's it, Toni?"
  
  Toni leaned over and whispered, "You know, I just went to the store, and then across the street, I saw Indra threw a big party. So many people come over to his place."
  
  I was surprised, "so you were saying that Indra intentionally didn't ask us over to his party?"
  
  Toni then tried to explain, "in some way, yes. But that's not the issue."
  
  "What, then?"
  
  "Okay. So, after I saw many people coming over to his place, I decided to join in. But when I was at the front door, I bumped into someone."
  
  "Okay, who?"
  
  "That was John. So, I asked them what he was doing there. Then, he said, 'Hey Toni, it's nice seeing you here. I knew you also got the invitation. Anyway, someone brought in some pizza. You're surely gonna love it.'"
  
  I couldn't care less about the invitation, but I didn't expect someone would brought in pizza to his house. That was too much.
  
  "That was just ridiculous, Toni. A pizza and Indra didn't even ask us over. That makes no sense."
  
  " Yes, that's true. But again, that's not the issue here."
  
  "Wh-what?"
  
  "Anyway, after I ate some slices of pizza, Indra and I had a little chit-chat. Then, we, including all the people at that party, decided to meet up at your place tonight. What do you think?"
  
  "What about the food? There are so many people, Toni."
  
  "Don't worry some of them will bring in pinapple pizza and beer."
  
  "W-well, if you say so."
  
  "Great, that means I have to ask more people over then. See you tonight"
  
  This month is not only boring, but also chaotic.

  Which one is best, the word "good" or "better"? The only correct answer to this is the word "good".
  
  I learned this logical fact from my own english teacher a long time ago, and still remember it well.
  
   Only the first form has a real value, a value of its own. The word "good" means something truly is good and not bad, and something "bad" has a real value of not being good. This means the two stairs on your board is not valid as it comes to value. Both the middle form (better and worse) and the number1-form(best and worst) has no solid value of their own, since they only refer to a comparison of some sort, a comparison to something else.
  Example: We are both really bad at this (the word "bad" showing the true level), still you are a little better and I am a little worse (the word "better" and "worse" here only deciding the LEVEL BETWEEN two really bad results/options. Hence, the "better" one of us, is still not at all "good". "Better" can often in reality describe something that is a lot worse than something "good". This is in fact often the case.

  Your and you're, there and they're - used to give me a lot of headaches. One time, about 12 years ago, my English teacher told me that you have to pronounce 'your and you're' differently. Your, I was told, must be pronounced as "Yo'r" and you're as "U'r", which didn't make any sense. And only a couple of months ago I finally figured this out, mostly by practicing and watching native speakers pronounce these words...over and over again. Now I can finally relax and be comfortable with how it supposed to sound. This "revelation" even boosted my confidence. 
  Advice for others: don't ever listen to non-native speakers, even if they teach a foreign language. At least don't listen to school teachers - they're the most incompetent of the kind. I'm sure there are teachers that do a good job at what they do, but in my experience, it's best to trust a book than a human (in these kinds of situations). Once you get enough basic education from a book, look up an online teacher - a native speaker, such as this awesome guy. :)

We are known for the thousands of bars we have in our city. So they call us "A capital dos bares" (The capital of the bars). And the very first bar that was biulted in our city is called.... Tip Top. It exists up to now and it was builted so the people who were working here  building the city, back in 1897, could have a place to have some fun, to get together and so on. The bar was created in 1929, so the people who go there today tend to be older. When you walk inside, you can see several pictures of the city in the early days.   How about silent "t" at the end of a word, "i don' know" for example
    ↳ **@JulioScheidt** (👍3 · 2019-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LzzJHwmQ_Oc&lc=Ugy5zoYmjepUkk5iLuZ4AaABAg.8oE99zjqbc-8oK7L7wfqq_
      'I dunno' (I don't know)
      I don't know what can I say >> I dunno what can I say.
      
      'I'm gonna' (I'm going to)
      I'm going to go to the mall >> I'm gonna go to the mall.
      
      'I gotta' (I’ve got to)
      I’ve got to go >> I gotta go.
      
      'Lemme' (Let me)
      Let me tell you about this >> Lemme tell you about this.
      
      'Gimme' (Give me)
      Give me what I want >> Gimme what I want.
      
      'Wanna' (Want to)
      I want to be free >> I wanna be free.
      
      'fraid = afraid
      'bout = about
      'til = until
      'cause = because
      
      I think that's it, I hope I've helped
    ↳ **@MABFR01** (👍0 · 2019-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LzzJHwmQ_Oc&lc=Ugy5zoYmjepUkk5iLuZ4AaABAg.8oE99zjqbc-8oF6lp8NfCe

      You've probably heard it in american accent,
      Actually in American accent there's a Rule for that 't' that, if it comes between two consonants it gets silent. 
      Therefore, i don't know becomes : i don' know or Usually :i dunno know

      🔥A trick of spoken English that my professor once told me: he said that when you are about to say the word "even" in a sentence, for example, a sentence involving the word "even" can be like this: "He doesn't even buy an apple." If you forget to say "even" at the start after the first subject then you don't have to worry about it. You can say the word "either" at the end of the sentence. For example you can say "He doesn't bring" and/or "He doesn't buy an apple Either". That will fully replace the mistake that seems to be made in the first sentence. That is a golden rule of spoken English.

      Here are some helpful professional expressions for working in restaurants:
      
      Greeting and Welcoming
      
      1. "Welcome to [Restaurant Name]!"
      2. "Good evening/afternoon, how many are in your party?"
      3. "Right this way, please."
      4. "I'll be your server today, my name is [Name]."
      
      Taking Orders
      
      1. "Can I start you off with something to drink?"
      2. "What can I get for you today?"
      3. "We have a special on [dish], would you like to try it?"
      4. "I'll put that in for you right away."
      
      Serving Food and Drinks
      
      1. "Here's your [dish] fresh from the kitchen."
      2. "Can I refill your drink for you?"
      3. "How's everything tasting so far?"
      4. "I'll bring you some extra [condiment] right away."
      
      Handling Requests and Complaints
      
      1. "I apologize for the wait, I'll check on your order."
      2. "I'd be happy to substitute [ingredient] for you."
      3. "Let me see what I can do about that."
      4. "I'll speak with my manager and we'll resolve the issue."
      
      Closing and Farewell
      
      1. "How was everything today?"
      2. "Can I bring you the check?"
      3. "Thank you for dining with us, come back soon!"
      4. "Have a great day/evening!"
      
      Some additional expressions:
      
      - "On the house" (complimentary)
      - "We're running a special on..." (promoting a deal)
      - "I'll be right back with that" (temporarily leaving the table)
      - "Can I answer any questions about the menu?" (offering assistance)
      
      Remember to always be friendly, attentive, and patient with customers!

  Pretty-good looks 
  Ugly-bad looks
  Wow-surprised
  Shop-a store for shopping
  Bottle-to drink from
  Warm-when in warm temperatures 
  Cold-when in cold temperatures

  Night-end of the day
  Goodnight-say when someone is about to go to sleep
  Morning-start of the day
  Good morning-when someone wakes up
  Bad-when u don’t like it
  Good-when you like it

  Baby-a young human
  Bed-where you sleep

  To grasp the straw( trying to succeed but what you choose isn't going to work

  His careless mistakes diminished him in the eyes of management.
  Fall flat -Said when a joke, idea or suggestion doesn't have the intended effect.
  For your attempts at mockery fall flat.
  Let's call it a joke that fell flat and leave it at that.
  Contradict- to say the opposite of what someone has said
  Her testimony contradicted the policeman's story.
  To contradict oneself 
  I can tell you everything you need to know.
  But I don't know anything about that.
  Contradict - of one fact or statement) to be So different from another fact or statement that one of them must be wrong.
  New evidence contradicts the established theories on this subject.
  Video appears to contradict Lauren Boebert's denial that she was vaping at 'Beetlejuice' show.
  Set foot in- to go to a place or enter a place (idiom

  Collocation
  Allocate resources 
  Allocate money 
  Allocate funds
  Allocate blame
  The city allocated money for disaster belief.
  The company's profits were allocated to its shareholders.
  To allocate for something 
  To allocate to
  Collaborate- to work with someone for a purpose.
  Followed by preposition- with on to in
  I collaborated with my friend.
  We collaborated on a project 
  We collaborated to create  new  guidelines.
  We collaborated in implementing the guidelines companywide.
  Generalize- to make a general statement that something is true in all cases based on what is true in some cases.

  Lose your mind- become mentally ill or crazy.

  Facilitate communication

**@PrachiSingh-vj2qy** (👍0 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=--4p-XpSBNM&lc=UgwRQT9-B07Prn0E96R4AaABAg
  I have noted your all words with examples to learn it and thought to share with others too......Thank you Aleena ma'am
  
  1.Courtesy words- Thank you, Please, May I, sorry, excuse me.
  
  2.Poised=(Calm) example-she remained poised during the interview
  
  3. Ethereal-magical quality in it, example- Madhuri Dixit's dance performances have an ethereal grace.
  
  4.Sagacious-having or showing good judgement and understanding. example-Sir Ratan tata is known for his sagacious leadership in building a trusted brand.
  
  5. Debonair-Charming(attractive personality)-James Bond is known for his debonair personality.
  
  6.Surreal-Dreamlike(beauty and nature)-The film Chak de India has surreal moments that captivate audiences.
  
  7.Seldom-rarely,not often, hardly(example)-I seldom do this, I seldom eat ice-cream, Seldom do we see such talent in young actor.
  
  8. Perhaps, Maybe(shayad)-Perhaps we can meet for coffee next week. The movie Laapata Ladies was so good that, perhaps, it will win an award.
  
  9. Ineffable-Indescribable in a good context, speechless, short of words(example)-Neeraj Chopra's performance was so good it was ineffable.
  
  10.Loquacious-being very talkative(example)-Kapil Sharma's loquacious nature makes him a great storyteller.
  
  11.Blossom-grow or develop(example)-His talent started to blossom once he found his passion.
  
  12.Sanguine-being positive in difficult situation, optimistic(example)-His sanguine outlook helps the team stay motivated.
  
  13.Languid-Weak, unenergetic, someone who doesn't wanna make an effort.(example)-Despite feeling languid, he still went to the gym.
  
  14.Veracity-Accuracy, or in simple words truthfulness, example-Veracity in reporting, he is known for his veracity in journalism.
  
  15.Meticulous-Showing great attention to detail, being very careful and precise. The designer was meticulous in creating her new collection.

  Dear Ben,
  
  I have been watching your videos for a year or so, and they have been very helpful :)
  
  Last year I had to take a Cambridge exam, because it was required from my home university in Milan (greetings for Italy!). It had to be at least a B2, so one thing that I found to be extremely useful to attempt the highest certificate - since I was spending some money anyway… -, without lowering my chances too much, was in fact to have my STARTING POINT assessed by an actual language school. It turned out that I was around C2 - according to their test - and so they gave me a mock test (which is 10 times cheaper than taking the test and definitely worth the expense, considering that the alternative would be taking the true test blindfolded!) for the CPE, which is, as you said, crucial to get an idea of the expected performance, should one take the actual test.
  I passed the mock, so they suggested I took no classes, and luckily it worked out and I have now the CPE :) But I agree 100%: many aspects of these tests are much more about STRATEGY than real competence, and to be fair I also had the great advantage that in my former linguistic high school we were trained specifically for some tests like the Goethe German C1 or the “IGCSE English as a second language”, and since these tests are very much alike one can sort of transfer the abilities for any other language.
  
  All the best, 
  And thanks again for your amazing work❤,
  Stefano

  The takeaway I keep coming back to is that opaque languages don't need a special method, they just need more hours. Polish took me twice as long to feel readable as Spanish did, and there was no shortcut around that. Just time.

      Learning language is as basic and just as crucial. You won't be delivering your keynote speech in English about astrophysics now either, if you need to learn English first.       Everyone is a child when faced with the unknown.   One thing I have discovered about grammar,  many try and study their target languages grammar in their L1,  If you want to ever truly master the language don't do that, read an overview of the grammar but don't study it in your L1 when you get to a level (through watching/listening/reading)  where you can start studying in your target language then study the grammar in your target language.   
  
  For example if you are learning japanese and you start off by studying japanese grammar in English later when you hit a higher level you will have to relearn a lot of that as japanese grammar doesn't fit nicely into english rules and definitions.   The same with thinking kanji/hanzi have meanings, they represent ideas, which is much different than a meaning.    This is one of the reason it takes so long the more you learn the more you have to relearn and align your thought processes.    The same in Thai.   I can only comment on those two but I assume it applies to any language not in the same family as you L1.

  I'm learning German. I'm listening to a Sue Grafton mystery like this: I'll listen to a chapter in English on one app. Then I'll listen to the same chapter in German on another app. I'm going through the whole book like that, chapter by chapter. I'm not advanced enough in German to understand the German really, but I catch words here and there because I know what that chapter was about. I'm catching some words that I "half-know" and becoming more solid on them. I'm hearing grammar patterns jump out at me. The book is mainly in the simple part tense, so I'm getting a lot of reinforcement on that conjugation. I think it's fun, too!

**@LanguageChallenge2026** (👍10 · 2026-07-29) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v5WkWmea3hw&lc=UgyWwIjNlE-HlMOOH9d4AaABAg
  This is exactly right. I've been learning multiple languages and grammar rules never stuck until I encountered them naturally in context — reading, listening, real conversations. The moment you stop "studying" grammar and start just noticing patterns in authentic content, everything clicks. The brain is way better at pattern recognition than rule memorization.

**@bertriksikken** (👍14 · 2026-07-29) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v5WkWmea3hw&lc=UgwFXSUZvqtEfJu-ncd4AaABAg
  For me personally (learning Arabic, Turkish) it's much more rewarding to discover/experience the patterns more or less by yourself and getting a feel for the language, rather than trying to memorize them from a grammar book. When having to speak completely consciously 'by the rules', I'd need 150% brain capacity, so I need the patterns/phrases to keep it workable, while I improve over time. I remember learning Arabic could be super annoying sometimes when getting corrected: you make a mistake, you already realize it didn't come out right, then get corrected extensively as if you didn't have the knowledge (completely breaking the flow of the conversation). I did have (most of) the knowledge but at the time of speaking I was just missing the skill to apply it correctly in time during the conversation. I help people practice my native language (dutch): I don't correct every little mistake with a lengthy explanation, usually  just repeat back the more natural/correct form and keep the conversation going. This way, I try to encourage confidence in speaking rather than punish someone for making mistakes. So I think my experience aligns nicely with the concepts from the video.

      A lot more than 150%.. working memory is 6 or 7 things. That's why people sit there lost in translation for extended periods of time formulating a response. When we speak our native language, it comes out in chunks, or patterns. That's why the US military and intelligence communities drill for four hours per day in patterns training up personnel for new assignments. They train to operational fluency in months with pattern repetition.

  You don't need to aim for perfect grammar. Native speakers occasionally make mistakes. In English, for example, it's very common to say "than me" when "than I" is correct; if the verb is intransitive, it's perfectly clear, but if it's transitive, it can convey the wrong meaning. Or they put "only" in the wrong place. In Spanish, I've heard people say one article, then choose a noun and correct the article.

    ↳ **@Thelinguist [channel author]** (👍0 · 2026-07-22) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oL2EwWQTP7U&lc=UgxGLwGccCbR1kE2k6x4AaABAg.AZKoTnWmdP3AZNGwOlQdnE
      From the LingQ team: "The teams are ranked by coins per member, not total coins. English has the most people and the most coins overall, but that total is spread across a lot of learners, so its per-person average lands it lower. Portuguese is 2nd because its average per member is higher, even though the total is smaller. Teams under 50 people are also normalized — not to give small languages a boost, but so that one person in a language with few competitors can't single-handedly earn so many coins that the other languages have no chance to catch up. You earn coins by reading, listening, and creating LingQs, with a different daily bonus multiplier each day."

  Steve, although I agree with you when it comes to the importance of exposure, and that language learning must be treated in a joyful and "natural" way, I don't really think that recall is bad for our learning process. Quite opposite, actually: recalling/remembering, especially when effort is required during this process, is one of the most powerful learning tools (if not the most), and there are tons of research that supports it (things like the testing effect, desirable difficulties, active recall, etc). By the way, recall is not necessarily restricted to just doing flashcards or drills; you can try to use the language when speaking or writing and this itself is a form of recall and a way to reinforce your networks of knowledge. The more you recall, the easier it gets for future recalling.

    ↳ **@Average1212** (👍0 · 2026-08-04) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mE3qTLUpBhY&lc=Ugy_mn9pKH63aUCs2sB4AaABAg.AZ39RwQygexA_1PsYbOrZh
      @Nicnacsqt  My recommendations for studying )take it for what it's worth, this is the opinion of a random guy on the internet)
      
      I do not recommend textbooks made in your native language at all. 
      
      If we are using Japanese as the example.   Learn the Kana, then the top 1000 kanji (that gives you 90% character recognition)  This is enough to start reading graded readers.    Then read, evry graded reader you can find on your level, watch youtube, watch CIjapanese videos, ken sensei, nihongo jikan, etc.   once your ability is up to a level where you can study grade 1 grammar in japanese then you can start using native japanese textbooks to learn the grammar if you want to take that route.
      
      English textbooks on japanese take a language that is fundamentally different that english and force it into english definitions.   If you are working towards full fluency these ways of thinking about the language that english textbooks teach you will all need to be relearned some day. and after a couple thousand hours of reinforcement that isn't fun. 
      
      If you feel you need to learn grammar then you do a high level overview just enough to be farmiliar that there are differences and the structures exist, but not instesive study and trying to master it, with a rough overview and reading+video you will build a better mental picture .

  Do NOT underestimate the power of a playlist. I have 4 povs, and I’ve moved onto editing the second book by now. I have a playlist for each character (that are all over 12hrs long at this point 🙃) and I think it’s actually a better alternative than just listening to an inspiration person/character talk before writing because the vibe of the music also helps get you into the headspace of the world, and let’s be real it’s a lot more fun to listen to songs that remind you of your little torture dummies than listening to someone talk lol. I can never forget whose pov I’m writing in because the music is constantly reminding me of them, and kinda works as a trigger of sorts for easy switching too. I just switch the playlist every time I move onto the next chapter and my brain fills in the blanks by now, highly recommend!!

  My novel has two distinct POVs, and for one character, I turned to the street forms of speech. She's street educated and learned to speak the common language on the streets. The second character has a more erudite manner of speech. My inspiration for the first character came from speech patterns of the midwest, where speakers frequently flip the use of "was" with "were" and similar terms. Having (informally) studied English language roots, I know that American English has an "upper class" manner of speech where more Latin-root words, and indirect patterns are used, and a "lower-class" way of talking that uses more Anglo-Saxon words and is much more direct. 😏

  Would you be willing to do a full-detail guide on how to discover/decide a main character's fear, desire, and misbelief, how to relate it to the plotline, and how to make a character arc from it?
  
  Context: I'm currently writing an adventure story (second genre undiscovered) in which the main character is a kid on a post-apocalyptic farm who wants to be an adventurer. His family, especially his father, will not allow this because of the danger (obviously), and he doesn't just walk out because deep down, it does scare him, the idea of being on his own, and he also knows he can't provide for himself easily. Then his home gets raided overnight while he was sleeping in a tree (no I won't explain why), the farm is burnt to the ground, and his parents and siblings are taken as slaves. His goal for the entire book is to pursue the massive raiding party and rescue his family, preferably by stealth, but catching up isn't easy, and multiple times he fails to rescue them when he does catch up, which brings the book to novel length (I hope). During his multi-month chase, he gets the chance that he always wanted to explore the world, to meet strangers, to make friends, discover secrets of history, and most of all, to learn that adventure isn't all it was cracked up to be. He makes friends with a kid from the raiding party, who ran off to join him after his first time trying to save his family. This friend teaches him combat and forces him to realize that sometimes in life you have to be cutthroat to do the right thing and help people, while the MC teaches the friend the importance of honesty, kindness, loyalty, maintaining a clean heart, and other such character traits.
  
  His desire is obvious, to explore the world. He dreamed of it for years. I think deeper down, there's more to it. He dreamed of the people he'd meet, and the friends he'd make. That's what he wants. He's also "just a nice, naive kid" who loves to help people and hates seeing others struggle. His fear and misbelief however, are proving elusive to me. Obviously they need to be a matter of the heart, deeply personal to him, but as for what I have no clue. And hopefully once I have them, the character arc should reveal itself.

      Hey! So most of my characters actually come from the same upbringing or trauma so to say. For me I explore how everyone reacts to the same situations differently. It is also impossible for everyone to experience the exact same thing even though it might be similar. So lean into those differences can create different world views. Personality is also a big thing because some people will naturally be more effected by things than others. For example, two twins could be abused in the same household but one might walk away with a pessimistic outlook on life while the other walks away thinking things can only get better. Or for example in my wip my characters all come from the same lab. One of them was mainly effected by lack of knowledge due to being separated from the world which leads to their curiousity. The other is more closed off due to fear, stemming from the same lack of knowledge my other character has. This one cause has two different effects because they are two different people.

      Anyway, wish you luck while writing :)

The female lead is torn between her noble duties/friendship with the Princess of Wales clashing with her developing feelings for her sea captain.  
  
  The status disparity between a noble lady and a naval officer and the reaction of society to their relationship is external plot.   3) Middle brother assassinates oldest brother, takes royal princess; forces marriage, king & queen killed; kingdom goes into a mix of civil war and anarchy.  MC wants to stop the civil war, but as middle brother is sending assassins after  him and duchess as well, he's trying to flee the kingdom to keep the duchess and himself safe.
  
  Some internal conflicts he's having include:
  A) Wants to be a leader of men, but often asks for advice from council or the adventuring party.
  B) Wants to be (and is required to be) chaste while celibate, but he gets distracted by the qualities of women. (Originally I had him get distracted by breasts, but my 'advisor' said to make it more vague and just use 'qualities of women.'  There are 3 females and 6 males in the adventuring party.)

    ↳ **@TheYunacat** (👍1 · 2026-07-31) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EIudiNhSyX8&lc=UgwhxDsbl9dBkZar8ch4AaABAg.AZsDk2xe9RXAZsu_oGAt6j
      I'm writing a D&D inspired story as well so this was interesting to me. (Mine is about a riches to rags noble sorceress who was at the center of a horrible accident and now runs from all her problems until she can't anymore).
      
      For yours, first I'll say your advisor was very correct, because just focusing on one thing like that comes across as shallow to readers and would defeat some of the purpose of that chatacter trait. Anyway, I think you have good worldbuilding so I'll say the one thing I kept asking while reading is, "Why is he a paladin?" and "Which deity does he serve?" His deity could certainly cause big restrictions for his actions or else he could potentially become an oathbreaker. Paladins get all their powers from their "faith" in their deity, so are there times where his faith falters and he loses access to that power for a little while? An example is he might be mid combat about to smite a foe but his internal conflict about the situation or people at stake causes his belief in his deity to waver and his magic doesn't manifest. Maybe that can also add to his want to be a leader because he's always following orders to something above, so it creates a little friction in how he might see himself on the food chain. Hope this helps and good luck writing! 😊

  This was really beautiful, especially the idea that backstory matters because it is still happening inside the character. That’s such a good way to judge a flashback. When we return to the present, something should feel different, even if nothing physically changed. I also loved the information gap idea, how one answer can quietly create a better question.
  
  It also made me think that the trigger doesn’t always have to be a smell, an object, or something very obvious. Sometimes it can be an emotion, a contradiction, or even the structure of two timelines. And some flashbacks hurt even when we already know the ending, because the characters in the past still don’t know it yet. Still, the main point is excellent: a flashback should put pressure on the present, not just explain the past.

  When I was learning German 🇩🇪, it took me some time to build the confidence to read a book. I was trying to read magazine articles very early. They were a bit easier in that they were shorter and I could choose to try to read something I liked and had some knowledge about already. The tabloid style 📰 were best because they generally do not use complex language. I could even work my way through "professional" material because they were shorter and focused 🔎 on a particular subject matter. 
  
  Later I picked up a Young Adult novel 📖. It was challenging at first. I started out looking up words, then marking them for later 🖍. After a while, I decided just to bulldoze my way though 🚧 because it was to much effort to keep interrupting the process. I found that as I continued, I understood more by virtue of exposing myself to the material. I could infer definitions by context and was so excited when I finished! 🎉

**@HomoSiliconiens** (👍100 · 2019-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pwIUBTwZ8Uo&lc=UgwjxgiAYwKkq487XrN4AaABAg
  I think I read a lot faster than most other people, even faster than average native English speakers. But I think this bad habit, reading fast, messed up my English. First off, I read fast because I want to get the contents of the books asap, which made me lazy looking up the dictionaries for correct pronunciation. I catch the meaning s of new words in the context of the text or passage instead of looking up for proper pronunciation.
  
  Also, I have to read the same book several times for I miss a lot at first or second round of reading.
  
  Reading fast helps to catch the overall contents of the books fast and efficient. But when it comes to scientific and technical subject matter, it only slows down and hinders my concrete and solid understanding. 
  
  I always advise my son to read slow, but diligently.
  
  Reading slow is not slow. It saves me tremendous time and frustrations. I always whisper to myself, "Tom, read slow, if you don't want to read it again!"

**@focuslee1343** (👍0 · 2019-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J622HQz79QY&lc=UgwYn9rDcnNf6BfSvwJ4AaABAg
  - "creature of habit". If you say that someone is a creature of habit, you mean that they usually do the same thing at the same time each day, rather than doing new and different things.
   - "break a habit". It means end , stop the habit. 
   - "force of habit". If you do something from force of habit, you do it because you have always done it in the past, rather than because you have thought carefully about it. 
   - "fall back into". It means that to go back to doing something or behaving in a way which you did before.
   - "old habits die hard". It means that it is difficult to end a habit.
   - "kick a/the habit". It means that end a habit or to give up something harmful taht you have done for a long time .
   - "break the habit". It is the same meaning of kick the habit.
   - "have an/the urge".

**@voltronsupremeFood** (👍9 · 2018-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gBEpjL_J7OU&lc=UgwbnbYNYwxLP2BOe_V4AaABAg
  I frequently rag on James, but I have to admit he does a many  things that will help you with  your conversations.  First notice he dresses well, So one thing to take is that you want to bring your best self forward.  He is dress dapper.  Two he is wearing a bow, while traditionally people-wear is a tie,  a bow can be used as an ice breaker in a conversation. It  helps other open up to you by acting as a conversation piece. Thirds thing is the empathy, instead of just saying aaahh you can invite them continue talking by asking them questions.  The fourth thing that James does is hand gestures.  The gestures are not over powering and flow with his tone of voice and hence make the conversation more lively.  Five knowing how to subtlety change your voices tone.   I do disagree on one point is the use of "OK" or "And"   because tone of voice is crucial, if you say ok with the wrong tone it can come off as sarcastic.  If you are unsure if your tone for OK is sarcastic or leading, then it better to not use OK and follow up with a positive leading question.   Follow these sets and you will come off as charismatic.  Remember too smile subtlety too, Like James does in his videos.  Compare James to the others on engvid notice that the others are uncharismatic and one could easily argue  extremely dull.

  Hi guys I'm an English huge fan and looking for lessons talking about wonder vs wander, are words that a commonly heard but a don't know how to use them, Can you help me please?
    ↳ **@werds1392** (👍0 · 2018-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qrYRDCty9y8&lc=Ugzu9Dk4yeYv6uCBwfB4AaABAg.8gL7tT2fLix8hW285YzSHX
      João Matamba Quimuanga basically wonder means to think about something. You could say, “I wonder what is going to happen tomorrow” or “I wonder what she is going to say.” Wander, on the other hand, means to walk around aimlessly or to leave the path you are supposed to be on. A runner who is competing in a race might “wander” off of the track, and that would probably cause the crowd to “wonder” what is wrong with him.  
      Edit: just a little extra information. Wander (as in walk around without a destination in mind) would be a good word to use if somebody is walking around a mall without knowing what store they want to go into.

    ↳ **@werds1392** (👍0 · 2018-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qrYRDCty9y8&lc=Ugzxpl8TiWi3qgKE7U14AaABAg.8gkLRL2ToCb8hW10wHcWUy
      Lutch Bizin in general, “checking something out” sometimes implies that the person doing the checking has never seen that thing before. When I load up my email, I usually say that I am checking it because I am familiar with my email account. If my friend tells me about a song I’ve never heard before I might respond, “okay, I’ll go check it out” before I go listen to it. 
      With all that said it’s important to stress that this is not a rule, it’s just something that can provide a guide in most situations.

  Mine is more of a commentary on the larger implications of American English. It is exactly the reason British English sounds infinitely more elegant - especially Received Pronunciation. In my opinion, new comers to the English language ought to, at least during the incipient stages of apprehending American English, understand the contractions that the language is replete with - like gonna, sorta, etc. I am actually fascinated that new learners of English are able to understand American English. British English by contrast is sympathetic to how the language is written, at least in the main. I speak and write Italian. Italians say of their language: Come si scrive, si legge. This simply translates: The way it's written is the way it's spoken. Good luck trying that with the English language. By the way, praises for your infusion of levity, jest and relaxed humor.
  - Godfrey Silas

**@juanfran579** (👍0 · 2022-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6pxUmP82aQw&lc=UgxSsFdFcP2vWfKC-XZ4AaABAg
  Strangely enough, I've come to the stage as a learner and teacher of English as a second language to make a distinction between sounding and speaking like a native speaker. Sounding like a native speaker means to me to get to a good standard pronunciation, being capable of modulating your voice naturally ( relaxed speaking ), making use of a wide range of vocabulary and , of course, showing a good command of grammar aspects as they come up in natural speech. Nevertheless, neither am I aiming at speaking like a native speaker nor am I pushing my students to do so. I mean it's up to you to take up a rather posh RP,  Glaswegian, Texas dialect or whatever standard or adaptation or not. I'd give my students the advice to keep sticking to what they identify with instead of turning into someone else. Ist's perfectly alright to speak good standard, no matter whether it's based on British, American or whatever guideline.

  Conjunctions like for, so because, and or are easy everyday words used to join words, clauses and phrases together.
  
  Correlative conjunctions join statements of related information.
  
  
  
  either or (choice)
  
  not only  but also(surprise)
  
  neither nor( negation)
  
  both and (including)
  
  
  
  
  
  conjunction pairs
  
  neither you nor you hairy-assed friend can come to my party.
  
  
  
  Conjunction examples
  
  
  
  1.They told me to either buy the shoes or put them back.(choice)
  
  2. Not only did it smell, but it also tasted funny.(surprise)
  
  3. The dog either ate nor slept that night(negation)
  
  4. Mr E. was both funny and modest about his adventures.(including)
  
  
  
  
  
  1, quizzes
  
  
  
  a.__2_ inclusion
  
  b.__4_ choice
  
  c.__3_ negation
  
  d.__1_ surprise
  
  
  
  1. Not only was it of great quality, but it was also cheap.
  
  2. Both the man and his dog were stupid.
  
  3. neither the woman nor the man were happy with the answer.
  
  4. Either you watch the program or we turn off the television.

  My character get put to 20 questions. Age, appearance, injuries, where they were born, what their childhood was like, friends/family, habits/hobbies, likes/dislikes, past jobs, and their hopes/dreams for the future (AKA their motivation). I end with this question: "In their own voice, what would they think about you writing a story about their life?" That's my first chance to write as them, to get into their headspace, letting them speak directly to me... often not being kind to me, haha! Although a few characters tried to flirt with me.

    ↳ **@Vampsailormoon** (👍3 · 2026-08-08) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CwcmwkEoMcU&lc=UgxjAnoV79mDY-O2Y5Z4AaABAg.A_A_icRy6lwA_CJjuoySWV
      not everything you consume has to be high art. tastes are varied. every book is going to have haters and fans. 
      I think learning to be okay with listening to criticism of books you like can help you to better understand your own tastes and develop a deeper relationship with books you read. sometimes the criticisms are valid. 
      like maybe the plot of a certain book really is silly and vapid. you can decide that, despite the fact that that might bothers other readers, it doesn’t bother you. You can acknowledge that it’s true, without having the same opinion about it as other people. I find that super helpful for when I’m reading reviews and deciding on whether I should read a certain book or not. If the one big problem most reviewers have with the book is something that I’ve learned doesn’t bother me, then that’s a good sign that I’ll like the book! 
      On the other hand, sometimes valid criticisms include pointing out something morally wrong that the author has done or written. that’s the kind of situation where, if you want to keep reading their book, you make sure not to spend your money in a way that would benefit the author, and apply a more critical lense to reading that author’s work from now on.
      
      there’s nothing wrong with you for enjoying things others might deem unenjoyable or “low quality”

  "Oh no, no, no. Why can't you run a little faster? Mr. Mishra will kill us if we're late again today!" she said, stopping for a second and turning back.
  Behind her, a girl stood far away, bent over and panting. She pushed her glasses back up to the bridge of her nose. "Oi, double battery, run faster!" the first girl shouted.
  "You can't be serious with me, Kiara," the girl with the glasses replied between breaths. "How can we be late again,bro?"
  Kiara made a skeptical face. "Well, can't blame you. All that studying at night is finally showing off."
  With that, both girls started running again.
  Kiara kept glancing back at Ruhi, laughing, and didn't notice where she was going. She suddenly bumped into someone hard. "Oh shi— sorry," Kiara blurted out.
  When she looked up, she was met with what felt like a soft wall of falling flowers. A basket had tipped over, petals spilling everywhere between them.
  She wanted to stop and apologize properly, but Ruhi grabbed her arm and pulled her forward."C'mon, we're getting late," Ruhi said urgently.
  "Sorry!" Kiara called out over her shoulder as they ran away.
  They reached the school just in time to see the guard closing the gate.Ruhi turned to Kiara, half terrified and half curious. "Kiara, we are so done."
  "Not so fast. Follow me," Kiara said, already moving.
  She ran to the other side and threw her bag over the wall.
  "Kiara, are we really doing this again? It's the third time this month," Ruhi said, glaring at the wall as her mind raced.
  "You got a better plan, huh?" Kiara asked.
  Ruhi shook her head. "Then follow me, smartass," Kiara said.
  Kiara jumped over the wall, with Ruhi right behind her. They grabbed their bags and sprinted to their classroom.
  Their professor, Mr. Mishra—a man in his mid-forties with round glasses and a very large forehead now lined with anger—was already standing inside."Oh, look, students," he said dryly. "Our great pupils, Ms. Kiara and Ms. Ruhi, have finally arrived. Mind telling us what got you so late, ladies?"
  Ruhi opened her mouth, unsure whether to apologize or make an excuse, but Kiara jumped in."Sir, we were on time, but—"
  Mr. Mishra raised an eyebrow. "But what, Kiara? Did a dog chase you, or did you both forget the way to school?"
  Ruhi's face went pale, but Kiara, sharp as ever, replied, "No, sir. A kid was stuck on a tree, asking for help. We helped him and got late."
  Mr. Mishra crossed his arms. "Oh, what a nice deed. What was the child's name, ladies? Tell me at the same time."
  Ruhi looked at Kiara, half terrified. Kiara pretended to stutter, giving her a hint. "Sir... that kid had a name something like b... b..."
  Ruhi took a breath, as if she'd understood—or decided to pretend she had.
  "Bunty!" Kiara blurted out."Ballu!" Ruhi said at the exact same time.
  The classroom fell silent. For a moment, neither of them moved. Then a few students burst into laughter.
  Ruhi slowly turned toward Kiara. Kiara slowly turned toward Ruhi.
  Mr. Mishra removed his glasses and pinched the bridge of his nose."Remarkable," he said. "Absolutely remarkable."
  The laughter only grew louder.
  "Not only are you late," Mr. Mishra continued, putting his glasses back on, "but you couldn't even agree on the name of the child you so heroically rescued."
  Ruhi opened her mouth, but Kiara beat her to it."Sir, actually—"
  
  "Enough, Kiara." She immediately shut her mouth.
  
  Mr. Mishra pointed toward the door."Both of you. Outside. For the entire period."
  Ruhi's face dropped. Kiara let out a dramatic sigh. "Sir, don't you think that's a little harsh for two brave citizens who saved a child?"
  Mr. Mishra raised an eyebrow. "Would you like me to make it detention as well?
  "Kiara straightened instantly. "No, sir."
  "Good. Outside."
  The moment the classroom door closed behind them, Ruhi rounded on Kiara. "Bunty?
  "Kiara looked at her as if she'd said something outrageous. "What do you mean, Bunty? You said Ballu!"
  Ruhi threw her hands in the air. "Because I thought you were saying Ballu!". 
  Kiara pointed accusingly at her. "I was clearly saying Bunty!"
  "You were stuttering!" Ruhi shot back.
  "I was giving a hint!"
  "It was a terrible hint!"
  Kiara scoffed. "Still better than Ballu."
  Ruhi gasped dramatically. "What's wrong with Ballu?"
  "Everything."
  Ruhi smacked her lightly on the shoulder.
  Kiara pouted dramatically as if Ruhi had done the ultimate betrayal to her."Ow! Violence! Now I
  know why Mr. Mishra punished us."
  "Shut up."Despite herself, Ruhi started laughing. A second later, Kiara joined in.
  From inside the classroom, Mr. Mishra's voice echoed through the door."I can still hear both of you."
  
  The laughter stopped immediately.A pause.Then the girls looked at each other. And burst out laughing again.

    ↳ **@dshufff** (👍3 · 2026-08-06) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iYxCRa3a8NA&lc=UgzHyXPS_OM914bQk_J4AaABAg.A_5NG-YsWpBA_7IF41MCCu
      This fear is not unfounded--and it's very good to be wary of AI tools that make big promises just to steal your work--but there are nuances. Never upload your paper to any platform unless you are on a paid plan that provides data privacy. E.g. The major American LLMs (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini) , as far as I know, don't train their models on your files/chats if you're on the paid tiers. If you're using a free tool/free plan, then that tool is absolutely taking your data for their commercial use in some form or fashion. I think the fear of someone wholesale taking your paper and publishing it in a journal is unlikely, but you still don't want an LLM feeding on your work. Even if you're on a paid platform, double check their policies about how they handle your data.

One thing from my native perspective, btw: "prevailing wisdom" is a bit formal sounding, like something you'd read in a school essay and some newspaper articles. It's correct and good to know, but if you want to use something a little less formal and more everyday you might also choose any of the following: accepted belief, conventional wisdom, traditional wisdom, popular opinion, general consensus, widespread view, etc. All of these sound a bit more modern and commonplace to my ears. **@Kei-p2u-e3s** (👍50 · 2025-11-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MZ0r2dcAqM4&lc=UgxpsRPEWKANBRpkKDl4AaABAg
  In this video, she talked about the Japanese tadoku method (extensive reading).
   I’m Japanese, and I have read a book about the Japanese tadoku method, so I would like to share my ideas based on the book.
  As she said, the point of the Japanese tadoku method is to focus on the amount of reading passages rather than reading intensive books.
   The merit of this strategy is that we can gain more reading experience and encounter words that were new to us.
   As a result, our vocabulary expands more quickly.
  In addition, this method has another advantage.
   It allows us to acquire the building blocks to think more deeply about various ideas.
   This is not only related to language learning but also useful for thinking in general, as well as for thinking more academically or about complex matters.
   This is because if we accumulate more and more ideas and vocabulary, weeks or even years later, that knowledge can become the spark for a new idea.
  The author of the book I read called this process “zyousei.”
   “Zyousei” means “cultivation” in English.
  I think this is very helpful for learning languages.
   For example, the knowledge I acquired a few years ago can suddenly become active vocabulary, allowing me to understand certain words’ meanings or nuances more deeply.
  Considering the above reasons, I think the Japanese tadoku method is extremely effective for language learning!

  I know one more rule:
  FISH / FISHES
  
  Fish = same kind or food
  Example: We ate fish. I caught two fish.
  
  Fishes = different species
  Example: The aquarium has many fishes.
  
  
  FRUIT / FRUITS
  
  Fruit = general meaning or same kind
  Example: I like fruit. / She bought some fruit.
  
  Fruits = different types of fruit
  Example: The market sells tropical fruits.

   𝙎𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙛𝙖𝙘𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙎𝙖𝙣𝙨 𝙎𝙥𝙚𝙘𝙩𝙖𝙘𝙡𝙚
  
  (𝓣𝓪𝓷𝓴𝓪, 𝓗𝓪𝓲𝓴𝓾, 𝓣𝓪𝓷𝓴𝓪 & 𝓗𝓪𝓲𝓴𝓾)
  
  
  An anonymous
  
  Helping hand feels twice too grand;
  
  Being vincible
  
  And much too invisible
  
  To feel deeply lovable.
  
  
  In dark, secret hours
  
  Whispering a sincere prayer
  
  Is the highest care.
  
  
  Be off the self-scoff :
  
  Satisfaction sans show off
  
  Is real self-care
  
  Happiness' receptacle
  
  Is content sans spectacle.
  
  
  The joy of giving
  
  Without telling it in text
  
  Makes one God —the next.
